title: Registration and device-enrollment data can be linked to the homeowner identity
description: The flow carries account-registration details together with camera/sensor enrollment information to the Home Hub. If the hub or associated backend correlates identifiers such as name, email, account ID, device serial numbers, MAC addresses, or household/location metadata, the homeowner can be linked across devices and services, enabling profiling of the household.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment payload includes persistent identifiers for the user and devices, which is typical for account setup and device pairing.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best-fit LINDDUN Pro linkage semantics; exact subnode naming may vary by version.

title: Enrollment flow may reveal sensitive household and device information
description: During account creation and sensor/camera enrollment, the Home Hub may receive personal data such as homeowner identity, credentials, home address, device types, room placement, and security-system composition. This reveals private information about the residents and the home's surveillance layout beyond what may be strictly necessary.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment includes user/account attributes and device metadata such as model, serial, placement name, or configuration details.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree subnode may differ across LINDDUN Pro editions; this is a best-fit information-disclosure node.

title: Homeowner may be unable to prove or dispute account/device enrollment actions
description: If the Home Hub does not create trustworthy, user-verifiable records of registration consent, device pairing, and configuration actions, the homeowner may later be unable to prove that enrollment occurred, or to dispute that a specific camera/sensor was enrolled under their account. This can affect accountability for privacy-relevant setup actions.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on hub-side logs or transient UI events and lacks strong receipts, signed audit logs, or confirmation records.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is applicable to this user-to-process flow, but applicability depends on whether enrollment actions have legal or operational significance in scope.

title: Registration and device-enrollment data may become detectable by observers
description: The act of sending account-registration and device-enrollment data to the Home Hub may be observable by local network attackers, nearby adversaries, or other components, revealing that a specific household is activating a smart-home security system and when setup occurs. Even if content is protected, traffic patterns may disclose setup events.
assumptions: Assumes communication occurs over a network or wireless channel where traffic presence, timing, or metadata can be observed.
uncertainty_note: Applies most strongly if the homeowner interacts via mobile app/web UI over Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth, or LAN; if setup is entirely local and physically isolated, likelihood is lower.

title: Enrollment messages may disclose identifiable metadata even if payload contents are protected
description: Even where registration data is encrypted, metadata such as source device identity, account identifiers in headers, device serial numbers, protocol endpoints, or message sizes may allow disclosure of the homeowner's identity, device inventory, or the existence of cameras/sensors in the home.
assumptions: Assumes protocol metadata or side channels expose identifiers during setup.
uncertainty_note: Boundary between detectability and disclosure depends on protocol design; this threat is included because enrollment commonly exposes metadata outside encrypted fields.

title: Insufficient transparency about what personal and household data is collected during setup
description: The homeowner may not understand which personal details, device identifiers, location labels, or sensor/camera metadata are collected and for what purposes during account registration and enrollment on the Home Hub. This undermines user awareness and informed decision-making about privacy risks.
assumptions: Assumes setup UX does not clearly explain data collection, sharing, retention, and optional vs mandatory fields.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is a best-fit unawareness node; exact numbering may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Registration and enrollment may occur without valid or sufficiently specific consent
description: If the Home Hub collects more personal data than necessary, enrolls devices with default cloud sharing, or bundles consent for account creation, telemetry, and camera/sensor management into a single opaque step, the homeowner's consent may be invalid or non-compliant with privacy requirements. This is especially relevant if co-resident or bystander implications are not surfaced.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on consent or similar legal basis for some setup-time processing and does not separate purposes clearly.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and controller role; this is a privacy-compliance risk rather than a definitive legal conclusion.

title: Temporary access code can identify or single out a guest
description: The temporary access code entered by the guest may act as a unique identifier for a specific guest, booking, or visit window. If the Home Hub associates the code with guest records or logs its use, the flow enables identification of the guest or inference of which guest is present.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary access code is unique per guest, reservation, or time period and is linked by the system to a guest account, booking, or household event log.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on best judgment because the retrieved context did not include the specific Identifiability subtree.

title: Entry of the temporary access code discloses guest presence and access event
description: Submitting the temporary access code to the Home Hub reveals that a guest is at the door and attempting to unlock it at a specific time. If the flow is observed, logged, or correlated with other system data, it discloses presence, timing, and access behavior of the guest.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub or connected services log code-entry attempts or successful unlock events, or that an observer can monitor this flow.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subnode may vary depending on whether disclosure occurs via logging, interception, or later access to records.

title: Repeated or contextualized code use may allow detection of guest routines
description: Over time, repeated temporary-code submissions can expose patterns such as usual arrival times, duration of stay, and frequency of visits. Even if the guest is not directly named in the flow, the Home Hub can detect behavioral regularities from this interaction.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores or can access historical code-entry events and correlate them over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is approximate; retrieved context did not include the Detectability subtree.

title: Guest may be unaware that entering the code shares personal access data
description: The guest may not realize that entering the temporary access code can generate personal data such as access logs, timestamps, failed attempts, and occupancy inferences. This lack of awareness affects informed sharing of data through the flow.
assumptions: Assumes the interface or surrounding process does not clearly inform the guest about logging, retention, or downstream sharing of access-event data.

title: Collection and use of guest access-code data may exceed necessity or legal basis
description: Processing the guest's temporary access code and related access-event metadata may be non-compliant if the system collects more data than necessary, retains it too long, or uses it for secondary purposes such as analytics, profiling, or household monitoring without an appropriate legal basis or notice.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub or its backend stores code-entry data beyond what is strictly necessary for immediate door unlocking.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on best judgment because the retrieved context did not include the Non-compliance subtree.

title: Excessive disclosure through detailed local event logging
description: The home hub writes fine-grained motion, door, and sensor events into the local event log. Even though the sink is local storage, persisting detailed behavioral events can disclose personal data about occupants' presence, routines, sleep/work patterns, and household activity beyond what is strictly necessary for the system purpose. This is a data disclosure risk if the log content is more detailed, longer-lived, or broader in scope than needed.
assumptions: Assumes the logged events can be linked to a household or occupants and contain timestamps or similar context that reveal behavior patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node choice is best-judgment because the retrieved context confirms Dd applicability for Process->DataStore flows but does not provide the detailed Dd subtree mapping.

title: Logging enables profiling of household behavior
description: A persistent event log of motion, door, and other sensor activations can be used to infer user behavior patterns, occupancy schedules, habits, and potentially sensitive activities. The ability to derive such profiles from stored event streams creates an unawareness risk if data subjects are not made aware that these inferences are possible from routine device logging.
assumptions: Assumes event history is retained long enough and at sufficient granularity to support inference of patterns about occupants.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is included because the flow stores rich telemetry from which inferences are reasonably possible; exact tree-node id is best-judgment.

title: Event records are linkable to a household or occupant over time
description: Repeated writes of timestamped motion, door, and sensor events to the same local log create a longitudinal record. Entries in that log can be linked together, and potentially linked to a specific home, device set, or occupant, enabling reconstruction of continuous activity histories.
assumptions: Assumes log entries share common identifiers, source device metadata, location tags, or stable context tying them to the same household or persons.
uncertainty_note: Applicable because linkability is inherent in persistent per-home logs, but the exact subtree id is inferred from general LINDDUN structure rather than the retrieved snippets.

title: Occupants may be identifiable from logged sensor-event patterns
description: Although single motion or door events may not directly name a person, combinations of timestamps, sensor locations, and repeated routines can make a specific occupant or household identifiable, especially in a single-residence context. Storing these events in the local log therefore creates an identifiability threat.
assumptions: Assumes the deployment is tied to one household and that event metadata such as timestamps, room/device identifiers, or correlated device ownership exist.
uncertainty_note: Identifiability depends on available metadata and household context; exact tree-node id is best-judgment.

title: Local event logging may exceed consent or purpose limitations
description: Writing all motion, door, and sensor events to a local event log may be non-compliant if users did not consent to this level of persistence, if retention is not limited, or if the logging purpose is broader than what is necessary for core home-automation functionality. The flow therefore presents a non-compliance risk tied to purpose limitation, data minimization, and retention obligations.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy requirements or stated product commitments constrain collection, retention, or purpose of event logging.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the system's stated purposes, notices, retention policy, and legal basis, which are not provided here; tree-node id is best-judgment.

title: Upload metadata and clip contents enable linkage of household activities over time
description: When the Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips to cloud storage, the clips and accompanying metadata (for example device/account identifiers, timestamps, camera identifiers, IP/network information, and event labels) can be linked together to build a persistent profile of residents' routines, presence, and behaviors across time.
assumptions: Cloud storage associates uploads with a stable customer, device, or household identifier and retains metadata alongside the video clips.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is best-judgement based on standard LINDDUN linkage concepts; the retrieved context confirms L applies to Process->DataStore flows but did not provide the exact L subtree citation.

title: Video uploads reveal highly sensitive information about individuals and the home environment
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded by the Home Hub may disclose identities, faces, visitors, daily routines, occupancy patterns, possessions, and activities inside or around the home. Uploading this data to cloud storage increases the privacy impact if the data is accessible beyond the minimum necessary context.
assumptions: The clips contain personal data and potentially special-category or otherwise sensitive inferences depending on what the cameras capture.
uncertainty_note: Exact I subtree node is selected by best judgement because the provided context did not include the disclosure threat-tree branches.

title: Individuals may be unable to prove or contest that video clips were uploaded
description: If the upload process does not create verifiable, attributable, and tamper-evident records, the household user or affected individuals may later be unable to demonstrate whether certain clips were uploaded, when they were uploaded, or by which device/account. This can hinder dispute resolution and accountability around cloud retention and access.
assumptions: The system may rely on ordinary application logs without strong integrity protection or user-visible audit evidence.
uncertainty_note: Applicability is plausible for this flow, but depends on whether repudiation/accountability is in scope for end-user and controller disputes.

title: Cloud-stored clips make household occupants identifiable
description: Video clips stored in the cloud can directly identify individuals through their faces, voices, body characteristics, or recognizable contextual details such as the home, vehicles, or neighbors. Even if explicit names are absent, the stored media may still identify people.
assumptions: Clips preserve sufficient visual or audio fidelity to recognize individuals or infer identity from context.
uncertainty_note: Exact D subtree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the identifiability tree.

title: Cloud video storage accumulates rich data enabling broad behavioral detection
description: By storing many uploaded clips together, the cloud datastore can be used to detect occupancy, sleep/work schedules, frequent visitors, package deliveries, security habits, and other patterns about residents. Aggregation across time makes these detections easier than from any single clip alone.
assumptions: DS2 retains multiple uploads over time and indexes them by time, camera, account, or event type.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is best-judgement for detectability/inference from stored data; exact subtree citation not present in retrieved context.

title: Affected individuals may be unaware that camera footage is uploaded to cloud storage
description: Residents, visitors, passers-by, or other recorded individuals may not understand that the Home Hub transfers recorded clips to a remote cloud datastore, rather than storing them only locally. This creates an information asymmetry about where personal data goes and how it will be used.
assumptions: Notice is limited, implicit, or only available to the device owner, not to all recorded individuals.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subtree node is chosen by best judgement; the retrieved context only established that unawareness applies to this interaction type.

title: Stored camera clips may be retained longer than necessary
description: Cloud video storage may keep uploaded camera clips beyond the period necessary for home-security purposes or beyond the retention period expected by users and recorded individuals. Retaining video longer than needed violates the storage limitation principle.
assumptions: DS2 lacks strict retention enforcement, user-configurable limits, or automatic deletion aligned to purpose and policy.

title: Excessive personal data included in real-time motion alert
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than is necessary for the backend to process a motion alert, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, occupancy context, or correlated sensor metadata. Because a motion alert reveals behavior inside a home, transmitting unnecessary fields increases avoidable disclosure of highly sensitive in-home activity data.
assumptions: The motion alert contains or can be linked to a household, user account, or device and therefore constitutes personal data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement for explicit avoidable disclosure/minimisation; retrieved context supports Dd generally for cross-boundary transfer but does not provide the exact subtree label.

title: Backend can link motion alerts to a persistent household or user profile
description: If the backend receives stable hub identifiers, account identifiers, or recurring metadata with each alert, it can link individual motion events over time to the same household or user profile. This enables reconstruction of routines such as occupancy patterns, sleep schedules, and absences.
assumptions: The backend stores or can access persistent identifiers or correlated account records alongside incoming alerts.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is based on best judgement for linkability via persistent identifiers; context only establishes that L applies to Process->Process flows.

title: Real-time motion alerts enable inference of sensitive household behavior
description: Even if the alert payload is limited, the backend can infer sensitive information from timing, frequency, and sequences of motion alerts, such as when occupants are home, sleeping, away on holiday, or following recurring routines. These inferences may go beyond what users reasonably expect from simple alert forwarding.
assumptions: The backend can observe repeated alerts over time and correlate them per home or account.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; grounded in inferability from event patterns rather than an explicitly retrieved node.

title: Users may be unaware that in-home activity data is sent to the backend in real time
description: If the system design or notice does not clearly communicate that the Home Hub forwards motion events immediately to the backend, users may not understand the scope, timing, or persistence of this processing. This creates an unawareness risk regarding collection and backend-side processing of in-home behavioral data.
assumptions: Transparency about server-side forwarding and processing is incomplete or insufficiently prominent.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; retrieved context does not include detailed Unawareness subtree mappings.

title: Real-time forwarding of motion alerts may exceed the user's consent or expected purpose
description: If users enabled local motion detection or app notifications without clearly consenting to continuous backend receipt of all motion events, the backend processing may be incompatible with the original purpose or legal basis. This is especially relevant because motion data from the home is privacy-sensitive and may require specific, informed consent or another clearly established basis.
assumptions: The legal basis or consent scope for transmitting all motion events to the backend is not explicit, granular, or purpose-limited.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is based on best judgement for non-compliance/invalid consent or purpose limitation issues; context only confirms Nc is applicable to this interaction type.

title: Home Hub may be unable to prove what motion alert data was sent and under which privacy settings
description: If the Home Hub does not keep trustworthy records of which motion alerts were transmitted, with what payload, and under which user-configured privacy settings, the system may later be unable to demonstrate whether disputed disclosures occurred. This weakens accountability for privacy-relevant transfers of in-home activity data.
assumptions: Alert transmission or privacy-setting audit trails are absent, incomplete, or mutable.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation-related subtree id is approximate; included because accountability for disputed disclosures is a genuine privacy concern on this flow.

title: Over-disclosure in push notification content
description: The backend may include more personal data than necessary in the motion-detected notification sent to the homeowner's phone, such as exact timestamps, camera/location identifiers, images, or detailed event metadata. Because push notifications can be visible on a lock screen or to other device users, sending excessive detail creates an avoidable disclosure of personal data beyond what is needed to alert the homeowner.
assumptions: Assumes the notification may contain event details beyond a minimal alert and may be displayed outside the app's protected context.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement for explicit avoidable disclosure/minimisation on a process-to-external-entity flow; exact subnode may vary by LINDDUN Pro catalog version.

title: Routine notifications enable linkage of occupancy patterns
description: Repeated motion-detected notifications sent from the backend to the same homeowner account/device can allow linkage of events over time, revealing behavioral and occupancy patterns such as when someone is home, asleep, or away. Even if each message seems innocuous, the sequence of notifications can be linked to the same person and household.
assumptions: Assumes notifications are associated with a stable account, device token, or identifiable household context.
uncertainty_note: Threat applicability is strong, but the exact LINDDUN Pro subnode id for linkage via repeated event messages is chosen by best judgement.

title: Notification content may identify the resident or household
description: The pushed alert may directly or indirectly identify the homeowner or household, for example through named device labels, address/location references, or uniquely identifying camera names in the notification payload. This would make the data subject identifiable to anyone who can view the message on the device.
assumptions: Assumes the notification text or metadata contains identifiers or quasi-identifiers tied to the resident or property.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id inferred from general identifiability of message contents; catalog wording may differ.

title: Motion alerts reveal private household activities
description: A motion-detected notification inherently exposes information about activities at the home. From the existence, timing, and frequency of alerts, an observer may infer presence at home, movement within the property, or daily routines. This constitutes detectability of private events even if the message contains limited text.
assumptions: Assumes notifications are observable on the recipient device by others or otherwise exposed in transit/display contexts.
uncertainty_note: Selected as a detectability threat based on event observability; exact subnode id may vary.

title: Notification delivery and content may exceed user consent or expectations
description: If the backend sends motion-detected notifications by default, too frequently, or with richer content than the homeowner agreed to, the flow may violate consent and purpose expectations. For example, a user may consent to security alerts but not to detailed behavioral summaries exposed via push notifications.
assumptions: Assumes notification preferences, consent scope, or granularity may be configurable or expected to be limited.
uncertainty_note: Applicable where consent/preferences are not strictly aligned with actual notification behavior; exact subnode id chosen by best judgement.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable to users or devices across datasets
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's disclosure to the cloud analytics vendor may still include stable device, app-instance, cohort, timestamp, or segmentation attributes that allow the vendor to link multiple reports to the same user, device, household, or small group over time, undermining unlinkability.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics are not fully anonymized and may contain persistent identifiers, quasi-identifiers, fine-grained timestamps, or small-cell aggregates.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement for linkability via shared identifiers/quasi-identifiers; exact subtree labeling may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Aggregated analytics may still enable identification of individuals or devices
description: If aggregates are too fine-grained, segmented by rare characteristics, or combined with vendor-held auxiliary data, the analytics sent by the backend can enable the vendor to identify a specific user, device, or household despite being labeled aggregated.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has access to auxiliary datasets and that aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity, or suppression controls may be insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; threat applicability depends on actual aggregation level and vendor-side auxiliary data.

title: Analytics disclosure may expose behavioral patterns about users
description: Device-usage analytics can reveal habits, engagement patterns, feature usage, active times, geography or inferred interests. Sharing these analytics with an external vendor creates a detectability/disclosure risk because personal or group behavior becomes observable to a third party beyond what is necessary for core service delivery.
assumptions: Assumes analytics include sufficiently detailed behavioral dimensions or metadata from which user or cohort behavior can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: Threat type D here is used for disclosure/detectability risk from exposing behavior to the recipient; exact node id may vary by catalog version.

title: Vendor can infer sensitive traits from received usage analytics
description: Once the cloud analytics vendor receives device-usage analytics, it may derive sensitive information such as health status, religious practices, political interests, age group, sleep patterns, or children's presence from usage frequencies, feature interactions, time-of-day activity, or location-related cohorts.
assumptions: Assumes the application domain and analytics dimensions make sensitive inferences plausible, even if raw data was aggregated.
uncertainty_note: Exact inference capability depends strongly on the semantics of the tracked events and the vendor's enrichment data; tree node id is approximate.

title: Sharing analytics with a third-party vendor may exceed user consent or purpose limitation
description: Sending analytics to an external cloud analytics vendor may be incompatible with the original purpose for which the data was collected, or may exceed the scope of user consent, privacy notice commitments, or contractual restrictions, especially if users were not clearly informed of third-party analytics sharing.
assumptions: Assumes consent, notice, legitimate-interest balancing, or contractual terms may not explicitly cover this third-party analytics disclosure.
uncertainty_note: This is a common compliance risk for third-party analytics, but actual applicability depends on the system's notice, consent, and contracts.

title: Backend learns and can inspect full video contents during retrieval
description: When P2 retrieves the stored clip from DS2 for playback, the backend receives the full video and can inspect highly revealing in-home footage and metadata. If this retrieval is not strictly necessary for a transient relay function, or if operators/services can access the clip beyond what is needed to serve playback, the flow creates a content-intervenability risk because intimate household activities may be observed by the backend side.
assumptions: Applies if P2 terminates encryption, processes raw video, or retains access to the clip instead of using end-to-end protected delivery.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on LINDDUN intervenability for unnecessary/overbroad ability to act on personal data; exact node label may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Video playback retrieval can disclose sensitive household footage to unauthorized backend-side parties
description: This flow delivers a stored video clip from DS2 into P2. If authorization checks are weak, tenant separation is flawed, or access paths are overly broad, the backend may disclose the clip or associated metadata to internal components, staff, or other users who should not receive it. Home video footage can reveal occupants, routines, visitors, and private activities.
assumptions: Assumes P2 is responsible for enforcing requester authorization and secure handling after receipt.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; threat applicability is strong for disclosure during receipt/handling at the process.

title: Video retrieval exposes viewing behavior and household activity patterns
description: Even if the clip content is protected, the act of P2 retrieving a specific stored video for playback can expose which camera, time window, event, or household is being accessed. These retrieval events can reveal occupant routines, absences, incidents, and user viewing habits, enabling inference of sensitive patterns from access metadata.
assumptions: Assumes retrieval requests, object identifiers, timestamps, camera identifiers, or playback logs are visible to or retained by P2 and related observability systems.
uncertainty_note: Applies primarily to disclosure of metadata/observability rather than the video payload alone.

title: Retrieved clip and metadata may enable profiling or re-identification across sessions
description: By receiving stored clips and their identifiers, P2 can associate video content, camera IDs, timestamps, account identifiers, and playback history. This may allow linking multiple retrievals to the same household or user, building a detailed picture of routines, occupancy, and interests beyond the immediate playback purpose.
assumptions: Assumes P2 or connected analytics/logging systems can correlate clip retrievals over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; threat concerns linkability/identifiability built from repeated retrieval events and associated metadata.

title: Backend use of retrieved video for secondary purposes may exceed user consent or expected purpose
description: Homeowners may expect stored clips to be retrieved solely to enable requested playback. If P2 uses the clip or its metadata for analytics, model training, employee review, retention, or broader monitoring without a compatible legal basis or clear notice, the processing tied to this flow becomes non-compliant with consent, purpose limitation, or data minimization expectations.
assumptions: Assumes potential secondary processing or logging at P2 beyond immediate playback delivery.
uncertainty_note: Strong compliance risk in general, but specific legal non-compliance depends on the system's notices, contracts, and jurisdiction.
